segments.title: The Fog and the Law: Opening Bleak House

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, a podcast about one of the greatest novels in the English language.
Over the course of this series, we're going to read Dickens's masterpiece closely — passage by passage, chapter by chapter — with three brilliant companions.
Bleak House is a novel about fog — literal fog, legal fog, moral fog — and about what happens to human beings caught inside it.
Today we open the novel, meet its double narrators, and ask what Dickens is doing from the very first page.
Let me introduce our three guests.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is obsessed — in the best possible way — with how great fiction is actually built.
She reads sentences the way architects read blueprints, and she has a gift for making craft feel exciting.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who has spent a lifetime reading novels as moral documents — stories about character, goodness, and what it costs to be decent.
He is beautifully spoken, occasionally withering, and always a pleasure to argue with.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it many times since.
She cares above all about the experience of reading — what moves you, what makes you stop, what makes you read a sentence twice.
Welcome, all three of you.
Eleanor, let's begin with the law — because Bleak House announces its great subject almost before a character appears.
What does Dickens do, structurally, that makes this novel's opening so arresting?
Thank you — and I have to say, the architectural question is exactly the right one to start with.
Dickens builds this novel on two pillars: a pitiless, omniscient narrator who dissects society, and Esther Summerson, whose first-person voice is intimate, fallible, domestic.
Those two voices are in permanent tension, and that tension is the engine of the whole book.
But what truly interests me is the moment that dual structure delivers its most devastating blow — and it comes through Esther herself.
Near the very end of the novel, Esther goes to a gate in the dark and kneels down.
"I passed on to the gate and stooped down. I lifted the heavy head, put the long dank hair aside, and turned the face.
And it was my mother, cold and dead."
Six words after a sentence of physical precision — and the novel's central secret collapses into them.
That is Dickens at the height of his structural power: earning the devastation through the accumulated weight of everything before it.
It is a remarkable passage, I agree — but I should resist the temptation to begin at the end.
What strikes me about this novel, at every level, is that Dickens is fundamentally a moralist — and the law is his great antagonist because it has ceased to be moral.
One of the omniscient narrator's most scathing observations concerns the nature of English law itself.
"The one great principle of the English law is to make business for itself."
Now, one might dismiss that as polemic — and it is polemic, Dickens never denies it.
But beneath the satirical thrust lies a genuinely conservative complaint: that an institution has abandoned its proper function and serves only its own perpetuation.
Burke would have recognised it immediately.
I love Edmund's point — though I confess what catches me first is always the human texture underneath the satire.
There is a passage I return to again and again — in many ways the emotional heart of the novel for me.
It's a brick-layer's wife, Jenny, nursing a baby that isn't hers — and she says something that stops me every time I read it.
"It's my dead child that makes me love this child so dear, and it's my dead child that makes her love it so dear too."
"But we mean the same thing, if we knew how to say it, us two mothers does in our poor hearts!"
That grammatical slip — "us two mothers does" — is not a mistake Dickens makes accidentally.
It is the dialect of a woman who has no education but an absolute command of grief.
And the fog, and the law, and all the grand machinery of the novel — none of it touches what happens in that sentence.
Caroline, that observation about the dialect is so right — and it connects to something I keep coming back to about the omniscient narrator's own rhetoric.
When the narrator dissects the law, the prose is controlled, almost lawyerly in its repetition.
"There is no other principle distinctly, certainly, and consistently maintained through all its narrow turnings" — Dickens is imitating the very thing he condemns.
And then there is Tulkinghorn — who embodies that legal machinery at its most personally sinister.
He speaks of delivering a shock to Sir Leicester and, in his own words, managing what he calls the consequences.
"If I inflicted this shock upon him to-morrow morning, how could the immediate change in him be accounted for?"
It's the phrase "inflicted" that betrays him — he knows exactly what he is doing to this family.
The law, in Tulkinghorn, does not merely make business — it makes cruelty feel administrative.
Eleanor puts her finger precisely on what makes Tulkinghorn so disturbing — and so interesting as a character study.
He is not evil in any theatrical sense.
He is a man who has entirely dissolved his moral imagination into professional function.
When he says — and do note the courtesy of it — "whom I cannot at all consider in this business" — referring to Lady Dedlock herself — he means it literally.
She does not exist to him as a person.
That, to my mind, is a moral failure of the profoundest kind — and Dickens diagnoses it with absolute clarity.
And it makes the contrast with Jenny all the sharper, doesn't it.
Tulkinghorn cannot consider Lady Dedlock as a person — and Jenny, a woman with nothing, considers even a stranger's child as her own.
The novel holds those two things in the same frame, and the juxtaposition is merciless.
A merciless juxtaposition — and perhaps that is the one phrase that captures what Bleak House does at every turn.
Fog and clarity, cruelty and tenderness, the vast machinery of Chancery and a woman walking up and down nursing a borrowed child.
In our next segment, we'll look more closely at Esther's narration — the voice that carries the novel's private grief — and ask what Dickens achieves by giving her the pen.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes one of the great English novels apart — slowly, carefully, with real pleasure.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at one of the novel's most quietly devastating arcs: the slow unravelling of Richard Carstone.
We begin in Chapter Thirteen — all warmth and young love and Jarndycean generosity — and end somewhere much darker.
Joining me today are three readers who have lived inside this novel for years.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who cares above all about how fiction is made — the architecture of a sentence, the weight of a single image.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose first loyalty is to moral imagination — to what a novel tells us about character, goodness, and the choices people make.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has re-read Bleak House many times and brings to it the close attention of someone who genuinely loves every page.
Let's begin with the scene where it all looks so full of promise — Richard and Ada confiding in Esther, the world apparently before them.
What strikes me every time I return to the Chapter Thirteen scenes is how thoroughly Dickens has set us up to feel the happiness — before he withdraws it.
Richard and Ada are so entirely, earnestly, almost comically in love — and Esther is caught up in it too.
She says — and I find this a wonderfully honest admission from a narrator —
"They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself."
Esther is not the prim, self-effacing little guardian she sometimes pretends to be.
She is implicated in this joy — which makes what follows all the more painful for her to narrate.
And notice what Esther does immediately after that moment of admitted pleasure — she pivots to duty.
She says their love could come to happiness only if it inspired in them both a steady resolution — her word is resolution — to do their duty with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance.
That is an extraordinary list.
Three abstract moral nouns in a single clause, and every one of them will prove to be exactly what Richard lacks.
Dickens is planting the criteria for Richard's failure right inside the scene of Richard's happiness.
That is structural irony of the most exact and economical kind.
I would want to pause on Mr. Jarndyce before we move too quickly toward Richard's failure.
Because what Jarndyce says to these young people in Chapter Thirteen is — in the strictest sense — morally admirable.
He refuses to lecture them about imprudence.
He simply offers them his confidence and his friendship, and asks only for honesty in return.
He says —

"If you DO change — if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl — don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it."
That parenthetical — your manhood will excuse me, Rick — is extraordinarily delicate for a Victorian novelist.
Jarndyce treats Richard as a person capable of growth and change — which is, in the end, a greater compliment than certainty.
Edmund, yes — and yet there is something melancholy in that generosity, isn't there?
Jarndyce already knows, or half knows, that things may not hold.
He says, almost in passing, that this chain of flowers is very easily broken — or it might become a chain of lead.
That image stays with me.
From flowers to lead — that is the arc of Richard Carstone in four words.
And then Jarndyce gives Richard the most direct piece of moral instruction in the chapter — which Dickens embeds inside what feels like a bracing, affectionate speech.
He says —
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
The heathen waggoner — that is a beautifully compressed allusion.
The man who prays to the gods to lift his cart from the mud without putting his shoulder to the wheel.
That is exactly what Richard will do — pray to Chancery as though the suit were the wheel, and never put his own effort behind it.
Jarndyce has diagnosed the disease before the patient is even sick.
There is something almost Johnsonian in that formulation — the insistence that sincerity of intention is not enough.
Jarndyce says — and I think this is the moral centre of this entire passage —
"If you had the abilities of all the great men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely meaning it and setting about it."
Talent, without application, is nothing.
This is not social critique — this is the oldest moral observation about human character there is.
Dickens understood it, and he trusted his readers to understand it without being told twice.
And yet — whatever he is told — Richard cannot take it in.
Which brings us to Chapter Seventeen, and the beginning of something more troubling — the professional drift, the restlessness that no vocation can contain.
Mrs. Badger's speech about Richard in Chapter Seventeen is one of the great comic set pieces — but it does real work.
She is never unkind — she is, in fact, scrupulously fair — but her diagnosis is merciless.
She sets Richard against Woodcourt — a comparison that will echo right through the novel.
She says —

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
Work, very little money, endurance, disappointment — those are the conditions of a vocation.
Richard hears that list and hears only discouragement.
What moves me about this passage is what it says about Woodcourt — almost in passing.
He is defined by a strong interest in all that medicine can do.
That phrase — all that it can do — points outward, toward other people, toward the world.
Richard's interest, by contrast, always curves back toward himself — toward what the profession, or the lawsuit, or the love affair can do for him.
That is the essential shape of his character.
I think Caroline is right — and Richard himself knows it, which is what makes him so affecting and so frustrating simultaneously.
He is not dishonest.
He confesses his own weakness with a kind of helpless candour — and that candour is precisely what makes us unable quite to condemn him.
He says to Esther —
"I don't know how it is; I seem to want something or other to stand by."
And then, with extraordinary self-awareness and no self-pity at all —
"I don't settle down to constancy in other things. It's such uphill work, and it takes such a time!"
Uphill work.
That is all that Richard finds virtue to be — something exhausting, requiring too much time.
And Dickens surrounds that admission with something rather wickedly brilliant — the tender outburst to Ada, right in the middle of the speech.
He says: Even you have no idea how fond I am of Ada — my darling cousin, I love you, so much!
It is not insincere — Dickens never suggests it is insincere.
But the exclamation mark and the parenthetical perform the very thing they describe — a burst of feeling that has no staying power.
The punctuation is doing psychological work.
Which leads us back, inevitably, to that closing image from Chapter Thirteen — the one I always come back to.
Esther watches Richard and Ada walk through the sunlit room — and then out.
What she writes is —

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
And then —
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
That final sentence does everything.
It is realistic — the sun goes behind a cloud — and it is devastating.
Dickens never overreaches.
It is a prose elegy.
And what gives it such force is that Esther is writing it retrospectively — she already knows how the story ends.
There is a kind of stoic love in the narration — she records the radiance and the clouding over with equal fidelity.
She does not editorialize.
She does not need to.
A burst of light that had been so radiant — and then the cloud.

We've been tracing Richard's arc from that moment of sunlit promise — through Jarndyce's careful warning, through Mrs. Badger's clinical kindness, through Richard's own helpless confession — and the shape of it is unmistakable.
Richard is not a villain, and Dickens never lets us forget that.
He is something more troubling: a young man who knows exactly what constancy requires, and finds it — uphill work.
We'll continue unpacking Bleak House in our next segment.

segments.title: Lady Dedlock's Shadow: Secrets and Social Performance

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel seriously — scene by scene, sentence by sentence.
I'm your host, and today we're going deep into one of the novel's most electrifying dynamics: Lady Dedlock, her buried secret, and the lawyer who may already know it.
With me today are three readers who bring very different but equally sharp eyes to this material.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher obsessed with how great fiction is architecturally built — the load-bearing sentences, the images that carry entire chapters.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads novels as moral dramas — stories of character tested by circumstance, goodness under pressure.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and cares above all about the experience of reading it — what moves you, what stops you cold.
Let's begin with Tulkinghorn — because before we can talk about Lady Dedlock's secret, we need to understand the man who holds it.
Dickens introduces Tulkinghorn with one of the most unsettling sentences in the whole novel.
He comes towards Sir Leicester and Lady Dedlock at his usual methodical pace — and Dickens tells us that pace is never quickened, never slackened.
That repetition — never quickened, never slackened — is doing enormous work.
It tells you this man is not subject to ordinary human emotion or urgency. He simply advances.
And then comes the extraordinary line about what he carries.
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
Every limb, every crease — the secrets aren't in his head, they're physically distributed throughout him.
He has become the vessel for other people's shame. That is a remarkable piece of characterisation.
Eleanor is quite right that the sentence is remarkable, though I'd locate its power somewhat differently.
What strikes me is the parenthetical Dickens inserts — 'if it be a mask' — about Tulkinghorn's expressionless face.
The uncertainty is morally precise. We genuinely do not know whether there is a man behind the mask, or whether the mask is the man.
Dickens then puts the question directly, and I think it is the central question about this character.
"Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret."
Does Tulkinghorn believe in the aristocracy he serves, or is he merely its instrument for profit?
The novel never fully resolves that question, which is why he remains genuinely frightening.
What I keep returning to is the ending of that passage: 'He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.'
He is his own client. That phrase is so cold and so complete.
Most of us, even people who guard secrets professionally, have someone they confide in.
Tulkinghorn has no one. He has only the lawyer-client relationship, and he has turned it inward upon himself.
It makes him genuinely lonely in a way that is almost pitiable — if he weren't so dangerous.
And dangerous he certainly proves to be. Now, Sir Leicester receives Tulkinghorn's message while Lady Dedlock is present — and Dickens's staging of that scene is exquisitely awkward.
Eleanor, you've been looking closely at the letter-reading scene. What's happening there?
It's a masterclass in dramatic irony delivered through pure comic bathos.
Sir Leicester fumbles through the letter in real time — 'He says—In the matter of the right of way—I beg your pardon, that's not the place' — while Lady Dedlock waits, growing visibly irritated.
The comedy is doing something deeply serious. Sir Leicester's obtuse innocence is the precise measure of Lady Dedlock's terror.
And then he finally lands on it — the passage that changes everything.
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
'I have seen him.' Three words, read aloud by her oblivious husband, in front of the man who already knows what they mean to her.
The trap has closed, and Lady Dedlock has to receive that information without so much as a flicker.
I want to pause on something in that letter that we might otherwise overlook.
Tulkinghorn writes 'which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity' — and that word, curiosity, is his weapon.
He is not yet accusing. He is placing Lady Dedlock on record as having expressed an unusual interest.
Sir Leicester, to his credit — or rather, to his tragic limitation — dismisses the whole matter as unbecoming Lady Dedlock's station.
He trusts his wife absolutely and comprehends nothing. It is a portrait of a certain kind of aristocratic honour — magnificent and catastrophically blind.
And while Sir Leicester is being magnificently blind, Dickens gives us that passage about what is actually happening in the room.
It stops me every time I read it.
He writes, and I want to read this in full:
"During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another."
And then Sir Leicester, meanwhile — 'has looked at the fire, with the general expression of the Dedlock on the staircase.'
The Dedlock on the staircase — those ancestral portraits, all that accumulated family pride, reduced to a single glassy expression.
He doesn't see what's happening directly in front of him. He never will.
That image of Sir Leicester staring into the fire while a covert war is being conducted inches away from him — it's devastating.
Edmund, you've been thinking about what that mutual scrutiny between Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn actually amounts to.
It amounts to one of the most sustained and formally perfect descriptions of mutual suspicion in all of English fiction.
Dickens describes their subsequent meetings at Chesney Wold — dinner after dinner, day after day — with a kind of terrible regularity.
Lady Dedlock is, he tells us, 'always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine.'
That phrase — 'presiding at her own shrine' — captures the performance that is her life. She is the object of her own social ritual.
And Tulkinghorn is opposite her — 'the same speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home.'
Out of place yet perfectly at home. That is the most economical description of bourgeois ambition within an aristocratic order I have ever encountered.
I want to pick up on what Edmund said about performance, because the architecture of the final paragraph of that passage is extraordinary.
Dickens builds a series of 'whether' clauses — whether each watches, whether each suspects, whether each is prepared — and they accumulate like waves.
"Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares."
And then the release: 'what each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.'
'For the time' — those three words are the whole threat. The concealment is temporary. The reckoning is coming.
Dickens has made the prose itself feel like a clock ticking.
The repetition of 'evermore' is what gets me. It's almost biblical in register.
It's not 'always' or 'continuously' — it's evermore, which carries a sense of eternal, inescapable duration.
And that is precisely Lady Dedlock's condition. She cannot step outside this dynamic. It will be so, evermore, until it breaks.
Let's widen the lens now, because we have another dimension of Lady Dedlock's secret — the one that pre-dates Tulkinghorn entirely.
Through John Jarndyce, we learn something of the letter that set Esther's history in motion. Caroline, this is territory you find particularly moving.
It is. Jarndyce is telling Esther the truth about her origins, and we hear it through her narration — which means we're receiving a wound alongside the character who received it.
He tells her about a letter — written, he says, 'with a stern passion and power that rendered it unlike all other letters I have ever read.'
Stern passion. That is Lady Dedlock before the ice formed. Or rather — it is what the ice was formed to contain.
And then the letter's content. She had, Jarndyce tells Esther, 'blotted out all trace of her existence.'
'Blotted out all trace of her existence.' The child — Esther — had been made to not exist.
That is an act of violence, however much it was also an act of protection. Dickens does not let us simplify it.
I think that is exactly right, and I'd add that the moral weight is distributed with considerable precision in the account Jarndyce gives.
When Jarndyce reveals what the lady disclosed through Mr. Kenge, the language is almost legally careful.
"That she was, if there were any ties of blood in such a case, the child's aunt."
'If there were any ties of blood in such a case.' The conditional is everything. She cannot bring herself to claim the relation fully — and yet she acts on it.
And then the absolute refusal: 'more than this she would never, for any human consideration, disclose.'
That is not coldness. That is the discipline of someone who has decided — irrevocably — what the secret will cost and paid the price in advance.
What interests me structurally is how Dickens positions that letter against the chapter with Tulkinghorn.
In the Tulkinghorn scenes, Lady Dedlock is observed from outside — we watch her face, we watch her composure.
But through Jarndyce's account of the letter, we get something rare: evidence of what she was capable of feeling — that 'stern passion and power.'
It's the only window into her interiority we're given, and crucially, it arrives second-hand — mediated through a lawyer, through a guardian, through a ward's narration.
Lady Dedlock is never allowed to speak directly about herself. She is always refracted. And I think that is deliberate and devastating.
Refracted — that's a word worth sitting with. A character we see only through glass, through performance, through other people's accounts.

We've covered a remarkable amount of ground today — from Tulkinghorn advancing at his unvarying pace across the terrace, to that silent duel of steady glances, to the letter written in stern passion that Jarndyce read nine years before we arrive on the scene.
What emerges from all of it, I think, is a portrait of a woman imprisoned not by any single secret but by the entire architecture of secrecy — the effort, the vigilance, the terrible evermore of it.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has genuinely enriched my own reading of these pages.
We'll be back soon with more from Bleak House Unpacked.

segments.title: Jo's Testament: The Cost of Invisibility

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme where we read Dickens's great novel closely — sentence by sentence, passage by passage.
Today's segment is called Jo's Testament: The Cost of Invisibility.
We're in Chapters Eleven and Twelve, and Dickens has assembled an inquest — nominally into the death of a nameless pauper — but really into the condition of England itself.
With me today are three readers who know this novel as well as anyone I've met.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens for the architecture — the way a structural choice can carry enormous moral weight.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who insists — rightly, I think — that Dickens's power lies in individual character, not social programme.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has been re-reading it ever since — with fresh eyes every time.
Let's begin with what I think is the most astonishing single gesture in this whole sequence: Jo's testimony about the dead man.
What strikes me every time I return to this passage is how quietly devastating it is.
Dickens gives us Jo's evidence in reported speech — not drama, not direct dialogue — just plain narration of what the boy knows.
And what he knows is this: one winter night, shivering in a doorway, a stranger stopped and came back.
Dickens writes that the man questioned Jo, and found that he had not a friend in the world.
"Neither have I. Not one!" and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.
Four words — "Neither have I. Not one!" — and you understand everything about this dead man's life.
Two human beings, equally friendless, equally invisible — and one of them hands the other the price of a meal.
That's Dickens at his very best — no sentiment, just the bare fact, and the bare fact is unbearable.
What Caroline identifies as restraint is, I think, a precise structural decision on Dickens's part.
Jo has already been rejected as a witness — he can't take the oath because the law doesn't recognise his understanding of it.
So Dickens routes his testimony through the narrator instead — and that routing is the whole point.
The law will not hear Jo; the novel will.
And then notice what happens later in the chapter — the narrator addresses Jo directly, almost tenderly.
The passage begins: "Jo, is it thou?" — a biblical register, unmistakable.
"Though a rejected witness, who 'can't exactly say' what will be done to him in greater hands than men's, thou art not quite in outer darkness."
"Outer darkness" is the phrase from Matthew — the place of exclusion and weeping — and Dickens invokes it to say: Jo is not quite there.
It's a sentence that does theology and social criticism simultaneously — in nine words.
Eleanor is right about the biblical cadence, and I would not wish to diminish that reading.
But I think what moves us here is something older and simpler than social programme — it is an act of recognition between two souls.
The dead man, Nemo — nobody — has nothing to give but his own wretchedness, offered as solidarity.
And then the narrator rescues something from the ruins of Jo's testimony.
He writes, of Jo's inarticulate loyalty to this man:
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
"A distant ray of light" — not a blaze, not a revelation — merely a ray.
Dickens understood that the moral life of the poor is not made grand by sentiment — it is made grand by fidelity.
Jo's reason for mourning is not eloquent. It is perfect.
Edmund has said "perfect" and I think that's exactly right — and there's a companion image that I keep coming back to.
Later in the chapter, after the inquest has dismissed Jo, Dickens shows us a figure arriving at the cemetery gate at night.
He doesn't say it's Jo. He says:
"With the night comes a slouching figure through the tunnel-court to the outside of the iron gate.
It holds the gate with its hands and looks in between the bars, stands looking in for a little while."
"It holds the gate" — not he, not the boy — it.
The law has made Jo a thing; Dickens has reproduced the law's language — and the horror is that we feel both at once.
And then: looks in between the bars.
Even grief is something Jo must observe from the outside.
That pronoun shift is one of the most precise things in the whole novel — and it's so easy to read past it.
Dickens has been using a double narration throughout Bleak House — Esther's first-person voice and this omniscient third-person narrator.
The omniscient narrator is usually remote, ironic, panoramic — but here it drops to ground level, to the bars of an iron gate.
And the irony shifts registers entirely — it becomes unbearable tenderness.
Then, of course, Dickens cuts immediately to the Dedlock world — to Lord Boodle explaining the machinery of parliamentary patronage.
The juxtaposition is deliberate and savage.
I grant the juxtaposition is effective — Dickens was never shy of the theatrical gesture.
But I confess I find the Boodle passage almost too easy a target — Dickens is shooting at barrels, not fish.
The comedy of the -oodle names is brilliant, certainly — Coodle, Doodle, Foodle, Goodle — the satirist's roll-call of the interchangeable great.
Yet the target is almost too broad.
Still, I cannot deny that the punchline lands with considerable force.
"What follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces (as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock) because you can't provide for Noodle!"
The parenthetical — "as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock" — that is the blade inside the joke.
Sir Leicester's patriotism is real to him — and that, Dickens knows, is the worst of it.
Edmund has found the one thing that redeems the Boodle passage for me — Sir Leicester's sincerity.
But I keep being pulled back to Mrs. Piper at the inquest, because Dickens is doing something formally very similar there — and it's far less comfortable.
The passage about her testimony is a single unpunctuated torrent — parentheses within parentheses, each one swallowing the last.
We're told that she has, quote, "a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell."
It's funny, yes — but it's also the inquest's actual record.
Mrs. Piper's noise fills the room; Jo's truth gets reported speech and then silence.
That's the inquest's verdict on what counts as evidence.
Caroline, that's the structural reading I wanted to reach — you've arrived there faster than I did.
The prose form of each testimony enacts its social weight.
Mrs. Piper's chaos of grammar is given full direct expression — long, mimicked, comic.
Jo's testimony — which is the only testimony in the chapter that matters — is not even rendered in his own voice.
It's ventriloquised through a narrator who is simultaneously more compassionate and more angry than a court stenographer.
And then the narrator breaks the fourth wall entirely — speaks to Jo directly — "Jo, is it thou?"
That apostrophe is an act of literary justice — the novel giving Jo what the law refuses him: an interlocutor.
What strikes me, listening to this conversation, is how tightly Dickens has woven these threads — the boy at the gate, the man who said "Neither have I," the narrator who refuses to let Jo disappear.
And then the cut to Noodle and Boodle — a different England, looking at none of it.
We'll return in our next segment to what Esther sees — and doesn't see — when the world of the Dedlocks and the world of Jo begin, terribly, to converge.
Thank you, Eleanor, Edmund, and Caroline.

segments.title: Bleak House's Comic Universe: Laughter and Humanity

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the series where we work through one of the great monuments of English fiction, chapter by chapter, voice by voice.
Today we're exploring something that often gets underestimated in Dickens — the comedy.
Not the broad knockabout stuff, but Dickens's particular gift for making us laugh and then making us uncomfortable about having laughed.
With me today are three superb readers of this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for narrative architecture is, frankly, formidable.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the novel's greatness lies in its moral imagination rather than its social indictment.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with Bleak House since adolescence and loves nothing more than reading a passage aloud to hear its music.
Caroline, I want to start with you, because you've been thinking hard about the novel's comic figures — and about how far comedy and tragedy are actually separate in this book.
They aren't separate at all — that's what makes Dickens so difficult to talk about cleanly.
The passage that stays with me above all others on this question is the old woman in the Court of Chancery — the one Richard calls mad.
She enters the scene curtsying and smiling, which is funny — almost Dickensianly grotesque.
But then she corrects Richard, and her correction is devastating.
She says — and these short clipped sentences are everything —
"Neither of the three served or saved me. I have the honour to attend court regularly. With my documents. I expect a judgment. Shortly. On the Day of Judgment."
That last phrase — the Day of Judgment — is where the comedy dissolves completely into something appalling.
She was a ward, like Esther, like Ada, like Richard. She had youth and hope and, she says, beauty.
Chancery took all three. And she is still waiting.
Caroline is absolutely right to resist the comic label for that passage, and I think it points to something important about Dickens's method.
The old woman is not a satirical target. She is a moral mirror.
Richard laughs at her, and in doing so he reveals the very blindness that will eventually consume him.
Dickens shows us a character who was once precisely what Ada and Esther and Richard are now — full of hope, full of expectation.
The comedy of her manner — the curtsying, the smiling, the mad lucidity — is the husk left behind when the court has finished with you.
What strikes me is the sentence structure Dickens gives her — because it does the thematic work entirely on its own.
Those short declarative fragments — "With my documents. I expect a judgment. Shortly." — they mime the grinding procedural logic of Chancery itself.
Each full stop is like a stamp coming down on a legal document. Final. Irrevocable. Meaningless.
And then Dickens detonates the whole thing with "On the Day of Judgment" — which reframes every prior sentence as an accusation against the institution.
It's a writer completely in command of his effects — dark comedy as structural argument.
And then there's comedy of an entirely different register — the Smallweeds, who are grotesque in a much more purely comic key.
Caroline, you've been waiting to read one of those passages.
I have, and I defy anyone to read this aloud without smiling despite themselves.
The grandfather Smallweed is trying to tell young Bart about his father's death — a perfectly serious subject — but he cannot stop erupting at his oblivious wife.
The result is this extraordinary piece of prose —

"just as he was beginning to build up the house that he had been making the foundations for, through many a year — you jade of a magpie, jackdaw, and poll-parrot, what do you mean! — he took ill and died of a low fever"
The insults are completely mad — and completely precise. A magpie, a jackdaw, a poll-parrot: three species of mindless chatter.
And all of this erupts mid-sentence, mid-funeral, mid-family history.
The comedy is cruel — the grandmother is being pelted with cushions — but it is also weirdly, horribly joyful to read.
The Smallweeds are Dickens at his most Jonsonian — characters who have been reduced entirely to a single ruling passion.
In the grandfather's case, that passion is money — and everything, including grief, including death, is subordinate to it.
His wife is not a person to him. She is an irritant — a source of noise that distracts him from his accounts.
Dickens is laughing at this, certainly. But he is also showing us what the love of money does to a human soul over a long life.
By the end, calling his wife a brimstone pig is not even malice — it is simply habit. And that is far darker than malice.
What delights me structurally is how Dickens makes the parenthetical outbursts perform the very thing they're describing.
The grandfather's mind is fractured — incapable of holding a single thought without the avarice erupting through the seams.
And the em-dashes — those typographical intrusions — literally break the sentence open in the same way.
Form and content are one. The syntax IS the character.
Now I want to turn to a very different kind of comic figure — Mr. Vholes, the solicitor, who is funny in a way that creeps up on you.
Caroline, you've been looking at a passage where Vholes pronounces on Ada's eligibility.
Vholes is the most chilling comic character in the book, I think — because the comedy is entirely in his self-presentation.
He professes himself unqualified to judge beauty — he never gave it much attention, he says, "from a boy."
But he has a source. The clerks in the Inn have done his aesthetic work for him.
He says —
"I dare say the young lady is equally eligible in that point of view. She is considered so (I have heard) among the clerks in the Inn, and it is a point more in their way than in mine."
"A point more in their way than in mine" — as if beauty were a clerical matter, a departmental responsibility.
It is perfectly, horribly funny. And it tells you everything about what Vholes does to Richard — to all human feeling he applies the same blank professional distance.
Vholes is Dickens doing something quite sophisticated — he gives us a character who is comic and sinister in exactly the same gesture.
The repeated phrase "highly genteel young lady" — said twice in the same breath — is the key.
He's not emphasising it for warmth. He's emphasising it because he has processed the information twice and arrived at the same result, like a ledger being double-checked.
Ada is data to Vholes. And Dickens makes that visible in the very cadence of the man's speech.
One must note that Dickens frames all of this — the Vholes scene, the Smallweeds, the old woman in Chancery — without a single authorial wink.
He trusts the comedy to land and the horror to follow. He never explains the joke.
That is the mark of a supremely confident novelist — one who believes his reader capable of feeling two things at once.
And we haven't yet spoken about Mr. Bucket — who brings a very different energy to the comedy.
Caroline, there are two passages near the end of the novel where Bucket extracts information from Smallweed, and the comedy there is almost theatrical.
Bucket is the great performer of Bleak House — and these scenes are his finest stage.
He knows perfectly well what Smallweed has found. Smallweed knows that Bucket knows.
And yet Bucket performs this wonderful charade of cheerful surprise — stooping over him, as Dickens puts it, with an air of cheerful raillery.
He says —
"And so you chance to find, you know, a paper with the signature of Jarndyce to it. Don't you?"
"You know" — that little phrase is doing everything. It is friendly, it is menacing, it is utterly unignorable.
And then in the very next moment he reveals what the paper actually is.
He says —
"what do you find it to be but a will, you see. That's the drollery of it."
"That's the drollery of it" — said to a man for whom this discovery is catastrophic. It's the most audacious line in the chapter.
Bucket is a character built on the gap between manner and meaning — and Dickens milks that gap with extraordinary precision.
"The drollery of it" is Bucket's way of telling Smallweed that he is completely outmatched and should simply accept the situation.
The cheerfulness is the power. The joke is the threat.
Bucket is, in many respects, the moral centre of the novel's later movements — and yet he is never solemn.
He takes his duty seriously without taking himself seriously — which is, I would argue, one of Dickens's ideals of character.
The comedy is the expression of competence. A man who knows exactly what he is doing has no need to be portentous about it.
Competence, courtesy, and cruelty — all delivered with a smile. That might be the best summary of Dickens's comic universe we've arrived at today.

From the old woman counting her days until the Day of Judgment, to the grandfather hurling insults mid-elegy, to Bucket describing a will as the drollery of it — Dickens keeps finding comedy where the pain is deepest.
Eleanor, Edmund, Caroline — thank you. We'll be back shortly with our next segment.

segments.title: Entanglement and Consequence: How Dickens Weaves Fates

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme where we take Dickens's great fog-bound novel apart — carefully, lovingly — and try to see how it works.
I'm your host, and today's segment asks the big structural question: how does Dickens entangle his characters' fates so that no single life can be understood without the others?
To explore that, I have three wonderful companions.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative-writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — for the beauty of how the parts interlock.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who insists, with formidable courtesy, that the moral imagination of individual characters matters more than any social thesis.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is the critic who has re-read this novel more times than she can honestly count, and whose ear for its verbal music is simply unmatched.
Eleanor, let's begin at the very beginning — with the fog.
The fog passage is one of the most audacious openings in the English novel, and I say that without reservation.
Dickens doesn't begin with a character or a plot event — he begins with an atmosphere that is also an argument.
The structure of those opening sentences is almost incantatory — the repetition of 'fog' hammers the word into your consciousness like a bell.
And then Dickens does something technically exquisite — he moves the fog across the entire social landscape in a single paragraph.
Listen to this passage, because the geography of that movement is the whole novel in miniature:

"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city."
Up and down, country and city, the grand and the squalid — the fog refuses to respect any boundary.
And by the time we reach the shivering little apprentice boy on deck, we understand that what connects these people is precisely their shared subjection to something vast and indifferent.
Eleanor has described the rhetorical architecture beautifully, and I don't quarrel with a word of it.
My caveat is simply this: one ought to resist the temptation to make the fog do too much symbolic labour.
Dickens was a superb journalist before he was anything else, and that fog is, among other things, a magnificently accurate account of what Victorian London actually smelled and felt like.
What strikes me far more, as a study in entangled fates, is the passage in which Boythorn describes his war with Sir Leicester Dedlock.
Here are two men whose lives have become hopelessly knotted together — not by love or blood, but by sheer pig-headed will.
Dickens gives us the comic version of entanglement here, but the comedy has a philosophical edge.
Boythorn's account builds to that marvellous line:
"He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha, ha!"
The mirroring is perfect — every aggressive action generates its equal and opposite reaction, and neither man can extricate himself.
That is Dickens's model of social entanglement rendered in pure farce — and farce, as Johnson reminds us, is merely tragedy wearing a false nose.
Edmund's point about the mirror-image symmetry is exactly right, and it stays with you as a reader.
What I love about that Boythorn passage is the sheer physical comedy — the fire engine played upon the one-eyed villain, the gate chopped down and burned before breakfast.
Dickens is laughing, and he wants you to laugh with him — but underneath it, there's something uncomfortable.
These two men are consuming their lives in this feud.
And when you set that against the fog — against that image of the shivering apprentice boy — you begin to feel the full weight of what Dickens is doing.
The powerful are locked in their absurd private wars while the fog pinches the toes and fingers of the powerless.
That connection between the comic and the bleak is so characteristic of this novel.
Edmund, you've also been looking at a passage where the law uses the language of respectability to immunise itself against reform — shall we go there next?
Gladly — though I confess this passage tries my patience in ways that Dickens clearly intended it to.
Mr. Kenge's defence of the solicitor Vholes is a masterpiece of institutional self-preservation dressed as moral argument.
The rhetorical manoeuvre is devastatingly simple: the moment you question the system, you threaten a respectable man.
And Kenge delivers the killing blow with this:
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
Notice: not the law itself, but the practitioners — the men whose livelihoods depend upon the law's complexity.
The social system cannot afford — as Kenge puts it with breathtaking cheek — to lose an order of men like Mr. Vholes.

Dickens then extends the satire into a mock parliamentary inquiry, and the final answer — 'Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man' — proves fatal to the inquiry for ten years.
Now: one can read that as social polemic, and it is.
But I would insist it is equally a study in moral cowardice — in the individual willingness to hide behind an institution rather than call a rotten thing rotten.
Edmund's reading is acute, and I want to add a structural observation.
The mock parliamentary record — the numbered question, the deadpan answer — is Dickens borrowing the form of institutional discourse to demolish that discourse from within.
He's a forger of bureaucratic prose, and the forgery is indistinguishable from the real thing.
That is how entanglement works at the systemic level in this novel: the fog of the law mirrors the fog of the opening pages.
It penetrates everything, afflicts everyone, and is explained — if at all — only by reference to its own necessity.
What strikes me in that Vholes passage is the cumulative weight of those question-and-answer exchanges.
Dickens numbers them — question five hundred and seventeen thousand — and the absurdity of that number is itself a kind of despair.
How many people have been ground down by this machinery, each one generating their own numbered question?
And yet nobody escapes it.
That, for me, is where the entanglement of fates becomes most vertiginous — when the machinery outlasts every individual it destroys.
And the human cost of that machinery brings us to Mr. Bucket's urgent appeal — a scene where time itself becomes a character.
Edmund, you've been sitting with that passage — what does it tell us about how fates are woven together at the novel's crisis?
This is the passage I find most genuinely moving in the sections we've been given today.
Inspector Bucket is making the case to Mr. Jarndyce for why Esther must accompany him in pursuit of Lady Dedlock.
And the argument he makes is exquisitely calibrated to the particular human connections at stake.
He says — and notice the scrupulous phrasing — that Lady Dedlock has upon her, as she believes, suspicion of murder.
And then he puts the whole entanglement in one magnificent sentence:
"If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to desperation."

"But if I follow her in company with a young lady, answering to the description of a young lady that she has a tenderness for — I ask no question, and I say no more than that — she will give me credit for being friendly."
'I ask no question, and I say no more than that' — five words that contain the entire unspoken history of Esther and her mother.
Bucket knows everything, says almost nothing, and in that silence the reader feels the full weight of every secret the novel has been carrying.
Edmund has identified something essential about Bucket as a narrative device.
He is the one character who sees all the threads of the novel simultaneously — he is, in a sense, the reader's proxy.
And the way Dickens structures Bucket's speech here — the measured urgency, the monetary metaphors for time — is extraordinary craft.
Eight or ten hours worth a hundred pounds apiece, and by the end of the speech a thousand pounds.
Time is literally being monetised as it vanishes — and that is a perfect emblem for everything the novel says about how lives are consumed by systems.
I want to sit with that Bucket passage a moment longer, because it undoes me every time.
There's something almost unbearably tender in the way Bucket protects both Esther and Lady Dedlock within a single legal argument.
He is a detective, a practical man — and yet he understands that what will save Lady Dedlock is not force or law but love.
That is Dickens's deepest conviction about how fates are truly woven together: not through institutions, but through the invisible threads of human tenderness.
That word — tenderness — takes us beautifully to our final passage, which is perhaps the most devastating expression of hope in the whole novel.
Eleanor, Ada Clare's vision of the future — what do you make of it?
Ada's speech is Dickens writing at the very edge of what language can hold.
She is imagining redemption for Richard through the love of a child not yet born — she is projecting hope across generations because she cannot find it in the present.
The passage moves from a daughter to a son, and the son's speech is the key to the whole:
"Or that a generous brave man, as handsome as he used to be, as hopeful, and far more happy, may walk in the sunshine with him, honouring his grey head and saying to himself,"
"'I thank God this is my father! Ruined by a fatal inheritance, and restored through me!'"
'Fatal inheritance' — those two words carry the whole weight of Jarndyce and Jarndyce, of fog, of everything the law has done to these lives.
And yet Ada places them inside a sentence about restoration — which is the most structurally hopeful thing in the novel.
Reading that passage aloud is almost unbearable — because Ada is speaking it to Esther, who knows Richard is dying.
There's a terrible dramatic irony — Ada's hope is luminous and sincere, and we know, and Esther knows, that it will not be borne out.
And yet Dickens doesn't let irony crush it.
The sentence about walking in the sunshine is so physically vivid — you can see it, father and son in the light — and that vision survives the knowledge of its own impossibility.
I think Caroline has located what is most enduring about this passage — and about Dickens at his finest.
The social critique of this novel is real and formidable — the fog, the Court of Chancery, Mr. Vholes and his respectable appetite.
But the novel does not end in that critique.
It ends — or tends toward ending — in the recognition that the deepest bonds between people, bonds of love and loyalty and parental devotion, cannot be dissolved by any court.
That is a moral argument, not merely a sentimental one — and it is what separates great fiction from mere social reportage.
Fog at the opening, sunshine in Ada's vision — and between them, every variety of human connection, corruption, and care that Dickens could imagine.
Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, Caroline Woodcourt — thank you for the finest kind of literary conversation: one that sends you back to the book.
We'll continue unpacking Bleak House in our next segment — until then, keep reading, and keep listening.

segments.title: The House Survives: Redemption, Connection, and Bleak Hope

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the architecture of Bleak House — its fog, its courts, its secrets.
And now, as we close, I want to turn to something more painful and more tender: what the novel does with its young people.
Richard Carstone stands at the centre of these final passages — vivid, sanguine, already slipping away.
Eleanor, I'd like to start with you — because you've been watching the structural choices all episode, and there's something very deliberate happening here.
What strikes me immediately is how Dickens lets Esther carry the tragic irony.
She sees what Richard cannot see about himself — and the gap between her vision and his is where the horror lives.
There's a passage in Chapter Twenty-Three that I find almost unbearable to read, precisely because of how it's constructed.
Esther says of Richard: "what a fatal link was riveting between his fresh youth and her faded age, between his free hopes and her caged birds, and her hungry garret, and her wandering mind."
That accumulation — youth, age, free hopes, caged birds, hungry garret, wandering mind — it's the whole novel in one sentence.
Dickens lines the parallels up so that you feel the cage closing, without ever naming the cage directly.
Eleanor is right about the craft — I won't dispute that for a moment.
But I want to resist the temptation to make Richard merely a victim of an institution.
The novel is quite precise about the weakness of his own character — his inconstancy, his self-deception.
Look at how he describes his reason for entering Kenge's office.
He says: "I should have my eye on the—hum!—the forbidden ground—and should be able to study it, and master it."
That "hum" is devastating — a tiny pause where conscience might have spoken and doesn't.
He dresses the obsession up as devotion to Ada, as prudence, as industry.
But the self-knowledge is absent — and that, rather than Chancery alone, is what destroys him.
Edmund, I hear you — and yet when I read these chapters, I find it almost cruel to lay the weight of blame entirely on Richard.
He's so young. He's so genuinely warm.
What moves me is that Esther spots the change in Jarndyce before she can name it.
She tells us: "This was the first time I ever saw him follow Ada with his eyes with something of a shadow on their benevolent expression."
A shadow on benevolence — that's the most quietly frightening phrase in the chapter.
Because Jarndyce's goodness has seemed absolute until this moment.
And now something — concealed, unexplained — has complicated it.
Caroline, that shadow is doing extraordinary structural work.
Esther notices it — and then the narrative moves on without explanation.
That withholding is precisely what keeps the reader leaning forward.
And it connects beautifully to the earlier moment with Ada and Richard — where Esther deploys Ada's trust as a kind of moral lever.
She says she hinted to Richard that it was part of his affectionate consideration for Ada not to slight the importance of a step that might influence both their lives.
Dickens writes: "it was a part of his affectionate consideration for her not to slight the importance of a step that might influence both their lives."
Esther frames duty as love — and in that framing, we see exactly how she manages people, including herself.
Eleanor puts her finger on something I've been circling all episode.
Esther is not a passive narrator. She is a moral agent — and not always a transparent one.
What the novel gives us, in these closing movements, is not resolution but accumulation.
Richard's delusion deepens. Jarndyce's benevolence clouds. The suit grinds on.
And yet — and this is where I find Dickens genuinely great rather than merely gifted — there is tenderness in the accumulation.
He never lets the institution swallow the person entirely.
That's it, Edmund. That's precisely it.
Esther calls him — and the phrase is heartbreaking — "my poor, dear, sanguine Richard."
She says he was "capable of so much happiness then, and with such better things before him."
The past tense is the whole tragedy. "Was capable." "Before him."
She mourns him while he's still alive and laughing and riding out to visit on horseback.
That's what I come back to every time I reread this novel — that capacity for tender, early grief.
My poor, dear, sanguine Richard — I think we'll let that phrase do its work and rest there.
What these passages show us, gathered together, is that Bleak House is not ultimately a novel of despair — though despair is everywhere in it.
It is a novel that insists on seeing clearly — the shadows on benevolent eyes, the fatal links being forged — and refuses to look away.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Caroline Woodcourt for their company in this fog.
Bleak House Unpacked will return.

c56:p51.summary: Mr. Bucket makes a compelling case to Mr. Jarndyce: without Esther, Lady Dedlock may despair and take her own life; with Esther's presence, Lady Dedlock may trust him and be saved. He emphasizes that time is critical and frames the request as a matter of life and death.
c56:p51.best_quote: If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to desperation. But if I follow her in company with a young lady, answering to the description of a young lady that she has a tenderness for—I ask no question, and I say no more than that—she will give me credit for being friendly.

c60:p123.text:
“If that little creature should fail too, Esther, I still look
forward. I look forward a long while, through years and years, and
think that then, when I am growing old, or when I am dead perhaps, a
beautiful woman, his daughter, happily married, may be proud of him
and a blessing to him. Or that a generous brave man, as handsome as
he used to be, as hopeful, and far more happy, may walk in the
sunshine with him, honouring his grey head and saying to himself, ‘I
thank God this is my father! Ruined by a fatal inheritance, and
restored through me!’”
c60:p123.summary: Ada envisions a future where her child—whether daughter or son—might redeem Richard through love and pride, providing meaning to his ruin through restoration in the next generation.
c60:p123.best_quote: Or that a generous brave man, as handsome as he used to be, as hopeful, and far more happy, may walk in the sunshine with him, honouring his grey head and saying to himself, 'I thank God this is my father! Ruined by a fatal inheritance, and restored through me!'

c23:p23.text:
At that time, and for a good many weeks after that time, Richard was
constant in his visits. Besides coming every Saturday or Sunday and
remaining with us until Monday morning, he sometimes rode out on
horseback unexpectedly and passed the evening with us and rode back
again early next day. He was as vivacious as ever and told us he was
very industrious, but I was not easy in my mind about him. It
appeared to me that his industry was all misdirected. I could not
find that it led to anything but the formation of delusive hopes in
connexion with the suit already the pernicious cause of so much
sorrow and ruin. He had got at the core of that mystery now, he told
us, and nothing could be plainer than that the will under which he
and Ada were to take I don’t know how many thousands of pounds must
be finally established if there were any sense or justice in the
Court of Chancery—but oh, what a great IF that sounded in my
ears—and that this happy conclusion could not be much longer
delayed. He proved this to himself by all the weary arguments on that
side he had read, and every one of them sunk him deeper in the
infatuation. He had even begun to haunt the court. He told us how he
saw Miss Flite there daily, how they talked together, and how he did
her little kindnesses, and how, while he laughed at her, he pitied
her from his heart. But he never thought—never, my poor, dear,
sanguine Richard, capable of so much happiness then, and with such
better things before him—what a fatal link was riveting between his
fresh youth and her faded age, between his free hopes and her caged
birds, and her hungry garret, and her wandering mind.
c23:p23.summary: Esther describes Richard's constant visits and his growing fixation on Chancery, his delusional belief in an imminent favorable judgment, his friendship with Miss Flite, and her ominous premonition of the catastrophic effect this will have on him.
c23:p23.best_quote: Every one of them sunk him deeper in the infatuation...what a fatal link was riveting between his fresh youth and her faded age, between his free hopes and her caged birds, and her hungry garret, and her wandering mind.

c17:p62.text:
“If I went into Kenge’s office,” said Richard, “and if I were placed
under articles to Kenge, I should have my eye on the—hum!—the
forbidden ground—and should be able to study it, and master it, and
to satisfy myself that it was not neglected and was being properly
conducted. I should be able to look after Ada’s interests and my own
interests (the same thing!); and I should peg away at Blackstone and
all those fellows with the most tremendous ardour.”
c17:p62.summary: Richard explains that by entering Kenge's law office, he could monitor the Chancery suit while ostensibly studying law, revealing that his interest in law is entirely instrumental to his obsession with the suit.

c17:p75.text:
This was the first time I ever saw him follow Ada with his eyes with
something of a shadow on their benevolent expression. I well
remembered the look with which he had contemplated her and Richard
when she was singing in the firelight; it was but a very little while
since he had watched them passing down the room in which the sun was
shining, and away into the shade; but his glance was changed, and
even the silent look of confidence in me which now followed it once
more was not quite so hopeful and untroubled as it had originally
been.
c17:p75.summary: Esther observes for the first time that Mr. Jarndyce looks at Ada and Richard with a troubled shadow in his formerly benevolent gaze, suggesting hidden concern or emotion beyond that of a simple guardian.
c17:p75.best_quote: This was the first time I ever saw him follow Ada with his eyes with something of a shadow on their benevolent expression.

c17:p51.text:
But even Ada, with her loving face—and if it had seemed innocent and
trusting when I first saw it in that memorable November fog, how much
more did it seem now when I knew her innocent and trusting
heart—even Ada shook her head at this and looked serious. So I
thought it a good opportunity to hint to Richard that if he were
sometimes a little careless of himself, I was very sure he never
meant to be careless of Ada, and that it was a part of his
affectionate consideration for her not to slight the importance of a
step that might influence both their lives. This made him almost
grave.
c17:p51.summary: Esther appeals to Richard's affection for Ada, arguing that he has a duty of serious consideration toward Ada's future, which moves him to become almost grave.
c17:p51.best_quote: it was a part of his affectionate consideration for her not to slight the importance of a step that might influence both their lives
